extracted.intended_audience: photographers, experimentalists, and statisticians interested in composite portraiture and demographic sampling (ethnologists, medical researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and methodological criteria for producing photographic composite portraits (apparatus, exposure, alignment, negative requirements, retouching) together with statistical-sampling and correction principles for comparing urban and rural population fertility/survival from census data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of portraits (aspect and lighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have the portraits of two or more different persons, taken in the same aspect and under the same conditions of light and shade, and ... bring them to the same scale, and ... superpose them as accurately as the conditions admit, then the different faces will blend surprisingly well into a single countenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraits used for composites must be taken in identical aspect (e.g. full-face or profile) and under the same lighting/shade conditions; otherwise blending will fail. Existing cartes-de-visite are almost certain to be useless because they rarely fulfil similarity of aspect and shade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate scaling and superposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the portraits to the same scale, and superpose them as accurately as the conditions admit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very careful adjustment in scale and position is essential; good composites cannot be made without very careful adjustment in scale and position. Off-hand ways of working produce nothing but failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fiducial lines and alignment points
rubrics_metrics.description: For convenience in enlarging or reducing, take care that the intersection of the vertical fiducial line with that which passes through the pupils of the eyes shall correspond to the optical axis of the camera. When the mouth is adjusted to the lower fiducial line, the scale is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use illuminated fiducial lines (preferable to black lines) whose brightness can be varied to match the portrait image; make the vertical that meets the pupils the optical axis so that enlargement/reduction leaves that point fixed, and use the mouth line to set scale accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer illuminated fiducial lines with brightness control
rubrics_metrics.description: It is far easier to work with illuminated lines; and it is important to be able to control their brightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce lines by a vertical transparency with a gas-light behind; vary burners until the image brightness is standard. A thin piece of glass set at 45° beneath the eye-hole reflects the illuminated lines to appear on the focusing-screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus construction and ergonomics
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus should be solidly made, chiefly of metal, and all the adjustments ought to work smoothly and accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the instrument so the operator can view and adjust everything within easy arm's length (eye-hole and sloped arrangement). Use rack-and-pinion movements for travel where possible; avoid occasional shifts of the plate by making adjustments with the plate in situ using a reflector/prism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflector/prism and focusing-screen arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Make adjustments while the plate continues in position with its front open through the help of a reflector temporarily interposed between it and the lens; do not use the ordinary focusing-screen but one flush with the roof of the camera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A swing mirror or a prism set into a sliding block will throw the image on a focusing-screen for adjustment and then be removed for exposure, avoiding movement of the plate and allowing convenient adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lens aperture choice (adjustment vs. photography)
rubrics_metrics.description: I find great convenience in a lens of wide aperture when making the adjustments, as I then require plenty of light; but, as to the photography, the smaller the aperture the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a wide aperture for viewing/adjustment, then a small stop for exposures. The hole in the stop used was two-tenths of an inch in diameter; one-tenth would be more suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiducial geometry for reflected lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A thin piece of glass immediately below the eye-hole reflects the illuminated fiducial lines in the transparency at f, and gives them the appearance of lying upon g,--the distances f e and g e being made equal, the angle f e g being made a right angle, and the plane of the thin piece of glass being made to bisect f e g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set distances so the reflected fiducial lines appear coincident with the focusing screen image; this gives accurate apparent registration for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding double reflections in mirror choice
rubrics_metrics.description: I chose my looking-glass carefully, and selected a piece that was plane and parallel. It has not too high a polish, and therefore does not give troublesome double reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a prism (perfect reflection) to an ordinary mirror when possible; front-silvered mirrors tarnish under gaslight and are less desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping the plate in position during adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: I avoid all this by making my adjustments while the plate continues in position with its front open. I do so through the help of a reflector temporarily interposed between it and the lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces risk of plate shifts that would spoil composite alignment caused by frequent replacement of the dark slide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure equality and order irrelevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The equality of the successive periods of exposure is shown by the equal tint of the four dots. The uniformity of resulting tint in the composite wafer is quite irrespective of the order of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If equal exposure durations are used for each component, resulting tints will be uniform and independent of the order of exposure. Demonstrated experimentally with a card and four exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted exposure produces dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: In making one of the composites I gave two-thirds of the total time of exposure to the first portrait, and one-third to the second portrait... the likeness of the longest exposed portrait always predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying exposure times allows controlling contribution weight of individual components in the composite; longer exposure = stronger influence on final likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size effects on composite stability
rubrics_metrics.description: They are real generalisations... The blur of their outlines, which is never great in truly generic composites, except in unimportant details, measures the tendency of individuals to deviate from the central type... numerical averages usually begin to agree pretty fairly when we deal with even twenty or thirty cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composites from small numbers show 'ghosts' of individual peculiarities; composites from ~20–30 or more cases give stable, repeatable generic images; larger samples idealise and regularise features (irregularities disappear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and rejection of components for typifying groups
rubrics_metrics.description: I selected out of 82 male portraits those that had more or less of a particular wan look... The selected cases were about 18 in number, and from these I took 12, rejecting about six as having some marked peculiarity that did not conform well with the remaining 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To elicit a particular physiognomic aspect (e.g. disease look), choose a subset showing the trait and reject outliers with marked peculiarities that would distort the composite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of composites for family likenesses (practical requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: All that amateurs have to do is to take negatives of the various members of their families in precisely the same aspect (I recommend either perfect full-face or perfect profile), and under precisely the same conditions of light and shade, and to send them to a firm provided with proper instrumental appliances to make composites from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negatives must be made purposely with uniform pose and lighting; amateurs' blemishes tend to vanish in blended results; young and old, both sexes can be combined into one ideal face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative format and scale requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: I use a repeating back and a quarter plate, and get two good-sized heads on each plate, and of a scale that never gives less than four-tenths of an inch between the pupils of the eyes and the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the head can be used as more distant parts (even the ears) become hopelessly blurred in composites. Make negatives at a scale giving at least 0.4 inch between pupils and mouth for sufficient detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional retouching and artistic use of composites
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional skill might be exercised very effectively in retouching composites. It would be easy to obliterate the ghosts of stray features... A higher order of artistic skill might be well bestowed upon the composites that have been made out of a large number of components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retouching can remove remaining stray features when composites are from few images; composites from many images produce faint idealised features that can guide an artist to draw final work with clear bold touches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing representative districts for urban-rural comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: It was important to choose well-marked specimens of urban and rural populations. In the former, a town was wanted where there were various industries, and where the population was not increasing... For specimens of rural districts, I chose small agricultural parishes in Warwickshire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single-industry towns or towns that have been increasing (immigration confounds results); choose samples minimizing atypical urban peculiarities to get a fair comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using census 'families' of young mothers to estimate living children
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mothers are young, the children are necessarily very young, and nearly always ... live at home. If, therefore, we limit our inquiries to the census 'families' of young mothers, the results may be accepted as practically identical with those we should have obtained if we had direct means of ascertaining the number of their living children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select mothers within a chosen age range (Galton used 24–40, notes he would prefer 20–35) so that census 'family' counts approximate actual living children without separate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply corrections for mortality and maternal survival
rubrics_metrics.description: I correct the results thus far obtained on the following grounds:--(B) the relative mortality of the two classes between childhood and maturity; (C) the relative mortality of the rural and urban mothers during childbearing ages; (D) their relative celibacy; and (E) the span of a rural and urban generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute adjustments for (B) child→adult mortality (important), (C) maternal mortality during childbearing (noteworthy), (D) celibacy (may be small), and (E) generation length (probably insignificant). Decide which corrections materially affect the comparison and apply appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparable life-tables for mortality correction
rubrics_metrics.description: The life tables of Manchester will afford the data for towns, and those of the 'Healthy Districts' will suffice for the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When local life-tables are unavailable, use life tables from similarly conditioned localities to estimate survival from childhood to maturity (Galton used 74% for Manchester and 86% for Healthy Districts for age 3 → 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rough-estimate procedure when detailed ages absent
rubrics_metrics.description: I am therefore obliged to make a very rough, but not unfair, estimate. The average age of the children was about 3 years, and 25 years may be taken as representing the age of maturity... 74 per cent. of children in Manchester, of the age of 3, reach the age of 25, while 86 per cent. of children do so in the 'Healthy Districts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exact child-age distributions are not recorded, approximate average child age and maturity age to estimate survival multipliers from life tables; be explicit about assumptions and their limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and possibly ignore negligible corrections (celibacy, generation span)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have no trustworthy data for the relative prevalence of celibacy in town and country... This difference of less than 1 per cent, is hardly worth applying... The possible difference in the length of an urban and rural generation must not be forgotten. We, however, have reason to believe that the correction on this ground will be insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the magnitude of each correction; small differences (<~1%) may be omitted if likely erroneous or acting in the wrong direction, but justify such omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulation and transparent arithmetic for final comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us now sum up the results. The corrections are not to be applied for (D) and (E), so we have only to regard (A) × (B) × (C)... In other words, the rate of supply in towns to the next adult generation is only 77 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly show numerator and denominator elements and the product of applied correction factors so the resulting comparative rate is transparent and reproducible.
